extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, journalists, communications students, and media critics
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for writing and evaluating press releases derived from Stuart Ewen's critique of public relations (PR as 'spin'), focused on honesty, transparency, and avoidance of manipulative practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish information from advocacy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A press release should clearly separate factual reporting from persuasive messaging; avoid presenting advocacy as neutral news. Anti-patterns: disguising promotional claims as objective facts or 'news'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose sponsors and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose sponsors and conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the source organization and any funding or sponsor relationships that could bias the message. Guidance includes naming the organization, listing funders, and explaining vested interests so recipients can judge motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manufactured pseudo-events
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create artificial events whose primary purpose is to attract media attention (a la Boorstin). Examples/anti-patterns: staged photo-ops, contrived 'launch' spectacles with no substantive news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge alternative viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include or at least recognize credible counterarguments or dissenting evidence rather than presenting a one-sided narrative. This builds credibility and allows audiences and journalists to assess balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't suppress unfavorable evidence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burying or omitting data and facts that undermine the release's claims. Anti-patterns: selective omission, cherry-picking results, burying caveats in fine print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about source motivations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the source is issuing the release (organizational goals, policy aims, commercial interests). Transparency about motives helps receivers evaluate intent and weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide independent verifiability
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims with verifiable evidence, citations, data sources, or third‑party corroboration. Guidance: include links to studies, public records, contactable sources, or methods so journalists and readers can check assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't exploit power imbalances
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leveraging organizational power to mislead or overwhelm less resourced actors; respect vulnerable stakeholders and avoid coercive messaging. Anti-patterns: using disproportionate access to media to drown out marginalized voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect audience autonomy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat audiences as capable evaluators: provide context, avoid manipulative framing, and do not attempt to unduly shape opinions through hidden tactics. Practices that undermine autonomy (deceptive framing, emotional manipulation) should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete context
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate claims within relevant background, limitations, and scope so readers can interpret significance accurately. Include methodological caveats, timelines, and relevant history rather than isolating data points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and avoid manipulative patterns (pseudo-events, manufacturing consent, spin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to and avoid manipulative patterns such as pseudo-events, manufacturing consent, engineering of consent, strategic framing, information subsidies, and 'spin' rather than information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book identifies patterns of manipulation—manufactured events, engineered consent, strategic framing, relying on 'information subsidies' to shape coverage, and general 'spin.' A press release should not employ these tactics; instead aim for factual clarity and openness. Examples: producing events primarily for media spectacle; crafting messages to manufacture public consent rather than inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not astroturf (fake grassroots)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating or presenting false grassroots support. Anti-patterns: paying or organizing false testimonials, creating fake social media activity, or otherwise simulating popular support to mislead press and public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't disguise advocacy as news
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to distinguishing information from advocacy but emphasized as its own violation: do not frame promotional or partisan messaging in a journalistic voice or format to mislead gatekeepers and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't manipulate public opinion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deliberate psychological techniques aimed at manufacturing consent or steering mass psychology (the 'engineering of consent'). Instead, present information that allows audiences to form their own judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't silence dissent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to marginalize, ignore, or suppress critics or alternative voices that are relevant to the topic. Practices that prevent dissent (intimidation, information suppression) violate ethical release standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty as a predictor of media uptake and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases that meet Ewen's ethical standards are more likely to build long-term media credibility, generate sustainable coverage, and survive scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ewen argues that honest, transparent releases avoid 'burning' sources and foster trust—practical reasons to adopt these ethical standards beyond their moral force. Use this as both an ethical and strategic criterion when evaluating release quality.
